title: The Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church
hookLine: an Eastern Catholic church outlawed under Soviet rule that survived underground

lines: A KITCHEN TABLE FOR AN ALTAR.
cards: A small apartment in Soviet Ukraine, late at night, the curtains drawn. A laborer takes a folded cloth from a drawer, spreads it on the kitchen table, and sets out bread and a cup.

A few neighbors come in quietly, one at a time, so no one notices a crowd. He is a priest, and this is the Divine Liturgy, sung almost in a whisper. Accounts from those years describe scenes like this.
Officially, his church does not exist.

teach.h: EASTERN WORSHIP, IN COMMUNION WITH ROME.
teach.b: The Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church worships the way Orthodox Christians in Ukraine do: icons, incense, the Divine Liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom, married men among its parish priests.
And it is in full communion with the pope. Greek in its name means the Byzantine tradition, not the country.

It is one of the Eastern Catholic churches, which keep their own rites and their own laws while belonging to the one Catholic Church. After the Second World War, Soviet authorities set out to erase it.
A gathering held under state pressure declared the church dissolved and its parishes joined to the Russian Orthodox Church. Priests who refused were sent to labor camps.
Its head, Metropolitan Josyf Slipyj, spent years in the camps before he was released to Rome. But the church didn't vanish.
It went into kitchens, forests and cemeteries. Bishops were ordained in secret; priests held ordinary jobs and served at night. Grandmothers baptized babies quietly and taught the prayers at home.

Catholics read those years through a promise in Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "where there are two or three gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." A kitchen table was enough.
As Soviet rule loosened toward its end, the church came out of hiding, and its people filled their churches openly again.

teach.h: THERE AM I IN THE MIDST OF THEM.
teach.b: It's a story with wounds on more than one side: Orthodox believers suffered under the same regime, and churches in Ukraine still carry that history together.
But the underground church kept the Liturgy going in the dark until it could sing it in daylight.

how: Ukrainian Greek Catholics celebrate the Byzantine Divine Liturgy in Ukrainian and other languages, in Ukraine and in parishes abroad, and honor the bishops, priests and laypeople who were imprisoned or killed under Soviet rule.

games.q: you're a Ukrainian Greek Catholic priest. the state has declared your church dissolved. join another church, you're told, or lose your freedom. what do you do?
o: refuse, and serve your people in secret.
games.why: under that pressure, many priests signed. those who refused were sent to labor camps or served at night, in kitchens and forests, until the church could come out of hiding.

practice: John Paul the Second liked to say the Church has to breathe with both its lungs, East and West, so take a slow breath and feel it fill both sides of your chest.

With each breath, let one Eastern Catholic church come to mind, even just a name: Ukrainian, Melkite, Maronite, Syro-Malabar, some living through war or exile now. If you pray, pray for them; if not, just hold them in mind.

wordCard.voice: Eastern Catholic. The Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church is one, of the Byzantine tradition, in communion with Rome, outlawed under Soviet rule, that survived underground.

carryVoice: Your line: the underground church. A kitchen table was enough. Until tomorrow.
